script.opening: "Mabel’s such a fussy eater — she’ll only eat a few things like plain pasta and crackers, and refuses anything new, especially vegetables. Mealtimes are a complete battle, I end up making separate meals. She seems happy and full of energy, but I’m worried she’s not getting what she needs. What can I do?"

facts.text: Mother, Kerry, on video; Mabel (3) is playing in the background, chatting to her teddy.

facts.topic: What she eats (if asked for a typical day)
facts.text: Plain pasta, crackers, bread, yoghurt, cheese, the odd banana and chicken nuggets. About 600 ml of cow’s milk a day plus "a couple of beakers" of juice; snacks on crisps when she won’t eat her tea. Refuses vegetables and anything new.

If asked: health visitor weighed and measured her at the children’s centre last week — "she said she’s on the same lines she’s always been on, about the middle". Red book shows weight and height tracking the 50th centile.

No vomiting, no choking or gagging on lumps, no diarrhoea or tummy pain, bowels normal. No rashes or reactions to foods. Lots of energy. Talking in sentences, plays with other children at nursery, no concerns raised about development or behaviour. No unusual sensory issues beyond "she hates sauce touching her pasta".
Born at term, healthy. No medicines; not on vitamin drops. No allergies. Up to date with jabs. Attends nursery 3 days a week, where she "eats a bit better".
Lives with Kerry and partner, Dean; baby brother (7 months). Kerry’s mother-in-law says Mabel "will end up ill" — adds to the pressure. Kerry was "a fussy eater" too.

Tired, anxious, wants to do the right thing. Admit "I’ve been pushing the vegetables hard" and offering pudding as a reward. Surprised and relieved when told she’s growing well: "Really? With what she eats?" Expect a blood test or supplements.

ice.ideas: "She must be missing vitamins, or something might be wrong with her."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "I dread teatime. I feel like I’m failing her." Criticism from her mother-in-law is fuelling the worry.

cues: "She seems happy and full of energy" — a thriving child; check growth.
"I end up making separate meals" — mealtime pattern to change gently.
"I feel like I’m failing her" — parental anxiety to address.

checkpoints.text: Confirms the child is GROWING/THRIVING (weighs, measures and plots growth against NICE NG75 thresholds, checks energy/development/wellbeing) as the key reassurance
Recognises picky/fussy eating as a common, usually normal developmental phase (food neophobia) and reassures accordingly

EXCLUDES red flags/organic causes (faltering growth/weight loss, very restricted intake/deficiency, dysphagia/vomiting, GI/allergy/coeliac, developmental or social communication concerns/autism — asking about talking, play and nursery — ARFID)

Gives PRACTICAL feeding/behaviour advice — family mealtimes/role-modelling, repeated low-pressure exposure, avoiding force/bribery/battles, realistic portions, limiting grazing/milk/juice, keeping mealtimes positive

Addresses parental anxiety, avoids unnecessary investigations/special supplements when thriving while recommending the standard daily vitamin A, C and D drops for under-5s, and refers (dietitian/health visitor/paediatrics) only for faltering growth/very restricted intake/red flags
Reassures and supports the anxious parent (it’s common, not poor parenting), and checks understanding of the feeding advice
Explores the mealtime battles and the worry about nutrition, and agrees a practical, low-pressure feeding plan the parent feels able to follow

Safety-nets and follows up: return if faltering growth/weight loss, very restricted range with nutritional concern, or red flags; growth monitoring and review — reassurance + practical advice, not unnecessary tests

worked.txt: "The most reassuring thing first — let me plot Mabel’s growth. … She’s tracking nicely, she’s active and developing well. That tells me she IS getting what she needs, even though it doesn’t feel like it at mealtimes."
"Picky eating at this age is incredibly common — toddlers are naturally wary of new foods. It’s a phase most grow out of, and it’s absolutely not a reflection of your cooking or parenting."

"Just to be safe — any weight loss, choking or vomiting, tummy symptoms or reactions to foods? How is she getting on with talking, playing and mixing with other children at nursery? … All fine. Good — that’s reassuring."

"A few things really help: eat together so she sees you enjoying foods; keep offering new foods without any pressure — it can take ten or more tries before a child accepts something; and avoid forcing, bribing or battling, as that backfires. Limit snacks, milk and juice between meals so she’s hungry at mealtimes, and keep them short and relaxed."

"Because she’s thriving, she doesn’t need tests or special supplements — but all children under five are advised to have daily vitamin drops with vitamins A, C and D, free if you qualify for Healthy Start; that’s standard for every child, not because anything is wrong. Try to step back from the battle; the pressure often makes fussiness worse."

"Come back if she starts losing weight or dropping off her growth, if her range narrows to almost nothing, or you’re worried about her development — then we’d look further or involve a dietitian. Otherwise, this should settle with time."

f.learning: PICKY/FUSSY EATING is very common and usually a normal developmental phase in toddlers/pre-schoolers (food neophobia), typically self-limiting, and the most important step is to confirm the child is GROWING and THRIVING — weighing, measuring and plotting growth on the UK-WHO chart (NICE NG75 faltering-weight thresholds) and checking weight/height tracking, energy, development and general wellbeing — because growth, not the food diary, is the key reassurance. Reassure the parent it is common, not harmful when the child is thriving, and not a reflection of poor parenting. EXCLUDE red flags/organic causes: faltering growth/weight loss, a very restricted intake risking deficiency, dysphagia/choking/recurrent vomiting, GI symptoms/coeliac, food allergy, developmental or social communication concerns/autism (sensory food selectivity; NICE CG128), or features of a feeding disorder (ARFID — extreme restriction/distress; DSM-5-TR, international) — which would change management and prompt assessment/referral. Give practical feeding/behaviour advice: regular family mealtimes and role-modelling; repeated LOW-PRESSURE exposure to new foods (it can take 10+ tries — keep offering without forcing); avoid pressure, force-feeding, bribery and battles (which worsen refusal); realistic toddler portions; limit grazing, excess milk and juice between meals; keep mealtimes positive, short and distraction-free; and involve the child. Address the parental anxiety and mealtime battles — a major part of the consultation — avoid unnecessary investigations and supplements when the child is thriving (but recommend the daily vitamin A, C and D drops UK advice gives all children aged 6 months to 5 years; Healthy Start for eligible families), and refer to a dietitian/health visitor/paediatrics only for faltering growth, very restricted intake with nutritional concern, or red flags. The skill is growth/red-flag exclusion, reassurance, practical feeding advice and parental support — not unnecessary testing.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG75 (2017) Faltering growth: recognition and management in children · [2] NICE CG128 (2011, updated 2017) Autism spectrum disorder in under 19s: recognition, referral and diagnosis · [3] NICE CG116 (2011) Food allergy in under 19s: assessment and diagnosis · [4] NICE NG20 (2015) Coeliac disease · [5] Department of Health and Social Care, Healthy Start and NHS vitamin advice for children aged 6 months to 5 years · [6] DSM-5-TR avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder criteria (international)
knowledge.summary: Fussy eating in a well, active 3-year-old is common and usually a normal phase. Weigh, measure and plot her growth, because growth is the real reassurance. Check for the few features that change management, give practical low-pressure feeding advice, and support the parent. Tests and special supplements are not needed if she is thriving, but the standard daily vitamin drops for under-5s are recommended for all children.

points.t: Weigh and measure (health visitor or recent clinic measurement), and plot on the UK-WHO chart in the red book. A child following her centile line is getting enough energy. NICE NG75 defines faltering weight by centile falls and a weight below the 2nd centile, and advises plotting length or height alongside [1].

Wariness of new foods (food neophobia) peaks in toddlers and pre-schoolers and usually eases with time. Many foods need repeated tasting before a child accepts them. It is not a sign of poor parenting.

Faltering growth or weight loss [1]; choking, gagging or pain on swallowing; vomiting, diarrhoea or abdominal pain; reactions to foods [3]; symptoms suggesting coeliac disease [4]; extreme restriction to a handful of foods of one texture or colour with distress, which may be ARFID [6]; and developmental or social communication concerns [2].

Eat together and model eating the foods; offer small portions of new foods alongside a food she accepts, without pressure; avoid forcing, bribing or praising only for eating; keep meals to a set time; limit grazing, juice and large milk drinks between meals, which blunt appetite; one family meal rather than separate meals on demand.

No blood tests are needed for a thriving child. UK advice is that all children aged 6 months to 5 years have daily vitamin drops containing vitamins A, C and D, unless they drink a lot of formula; Healthy Start vitamins are free to eligible families [5].

Refer or involve the health visitor, dietitian or paediatrics for faltering growth [1], very restricted intake with a risk of deficiency, suspected ARFID, suspected allergy, or developmental concerns [2]. Otherwise, the health visitor is a useful first contact for feeding support.

After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Practical low-pressure feeding advice agreed with the parent; standard daily vitamin drops for under-5s.
Addresses parental anxiety and family meals; health visitor support.
Return for weight loss, falling centiles, a narrowing diet, choking or developmental concerns; growth recheck.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picks up “she seems happy and full of energy” as a key reassurance and “I’m worried she’s not getting what she needs” as the concern.
Idea (missing vitamins or something wrong), concern (nutrition), expectation (blood tests or supplements).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I dread teatime. I feel like I’m failing her." Criticism from her mother-in-law is fuelling the worry — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Shah. And hello, Mabel. What brings you both in today?

Mabel’s such a fussy eater. She’ll only eat a few things like plain pasta and crackers, and refuses anything new, especially vegetables. Mealtimes are a complete battle; I end up making separate meals. She seems happy and full of energy, but I’m worried she’s not getting what she needs. What can I do?
That sounds exhausting, day after day. I can see you’re working hard to feed her well. Can I ask some questions, look at her red book, and then we’ll make a plan together?
model.why: Validates effort and sets the agenda

model.text: Yes, please.
Talk me through a typical day of what she eats and drinks, including milk, juice and snacks.
model.why: Food and drink history, including grazing and milk

model.text: Pasta, crackers, a bit of bread, yoghurt. She has milk and some juice, and she snacks when she won’t eat her tea.
Has she ever choked, gagged a lot, or had pain when swallowing? Any vomiting, diarrhoea or tummy pain?
model.why: Screens swallowing and GI red flags

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Has any food ever caused a rash, swelling or sickness?
No, never.
How is she getting on with talking, playing and mixing with other children? Any worries from nursery or the health visitor?
No, she chats all day and plays well. Nobody’s mentioned anything.
When she’s offered something new, does she get very distressed, or just say no?
model.why: Distinguishes ordinary fussiness from ARFID-type distress

model.text: She just says no and pushes it away. Then it becomes a battle.
How are the battles affecting you and the rest of the family?
I dread teatime. I feel like I’m failing her.
You’re clearly not failing her; you’re here because you care. What do you think might be going on, and what worries you most?
I worry she’s missing vitamins or something’s wrong with her. I thought maybe she needs a blood test or supplements.
Thank you, that’s really helpful. Could you hold her red book up to the camera — the health visitor’s weight and height from last week and the growth chart will tell us a lot.
model.why: Links the worry to the key test

model.text: Mabel is following her growth lines nicely for weight and height, and she looks well and active. That tells me she is getting what she needs, even though mealtimes don’t feel that way.
model.why: Growth plotted as the key reassurance

model.text: Really? With what she eats?

Yes. Being wary of new foods is very common at this age. It usually improves as children get older, and it’s nothing to do with your cooking or parenting. And because she’s growing well and has none of the warning signs, she doesn’t need blood tests.
That’s such a relief.

Here are some things that often help. Eat together when you can, so she sees you enjoying different foods. Put a small amount of a new food on her plate next to something she likes, and don’t press her to eat it. Children often need many tries before they accept a food. Which of these feels doable at your house?
Eating together, yes. I’ve been pushing the vegetables hard.

Stepping back from the pushing is one of the most helpful things. Pressure, bribes and battles tend to make refusal worse. Keep meals short and calm, and let her decide how much she eats from what’s offered.
And the separate meals?

Try one family meal that includes at least one food she usually eats. Snacks, milk and juice between meals fill her up, so set times for snacks and offer water between meals. She’ll come to the table hungrier.
model.why: Limits grazing, milk and juice; one family meal

model.text: That makes sense.

On supplements: all children under five are advised to have daily vitamin drops with vitamins A, C and D. If you qualify for Healthy Start, they’re free. That’s standard for every child, not because anything is wrong.
model.why: Correct UK vitamin advice without over-medicalising

model.text: Please come back if she loses weight or drops off her growth lines, if the foods she eats narrow to almost nothing, if she chokes or vomits with food, or if you have worries about her development. The health visitor can also help and recheck her growth in a few months.
Okay.
What are the main things you’ll try at home?
Eat together, a tiny bit of new food with no pressure, no bribes, set snack times and fewer drinks between meals, and daily vitamin drops.
Perfect. You’re doing a good job; this phase usually settles.

social.t: Daily mealtime battles strain the whole family. Reducing pressure helps the parent as much as the child.
Making separate meals and throwing food away costs money. Healthy Start can provide free vitamins and help buying food for eligible families.

legal.t: A parent with parental responsibility consents for a 3-year-old. Speak to Mabel directly on the call in a way she understands.

professional.t: Reassurance based on plotted growth is evidence, not dismissal. Record the measurements and centiles.
The health visiting team offers feeding support and growth checks, and should hear about any concern about growth or development.

community.t: Health visitors and children’s centres run feeding and parenting support. The NHS Start for Life website has advice on fussy eating.

redFlags: Faltering growth or weight loss (NICE NG75)
Choking, gagging, pain on swallowing, vomiting, diarrhoea
Reactions to foods (NICE CG116); coeliac symptoms (NICE NG20)
Extreme restriction with distress (possible ARFID); developmental or social communication concerns (NICE CG128)
ice: Idea: she is missing vitamins or something is wrong
Concern: she is not getting enough nutrition

playbook.diagnosis: “This is normal fussy eating in a child who is growing well and developing normally.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Young children are programmed to be wary of new foods, a bit like a smoke alarm that goes off at anything unfamiliar. Each calm, no-pressure meeting with a food teaches the alarm it’s safe. Pushing sets the alarm off again.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried she isn’t getting enough and might need tests. Her growth chart shows she is getting what she needs, so she doesn’t need tests. What will help most is making mealtimes calmer.”
management.psychosocial: Relieve guilt, reduce the battles, and pick one or two changes the parent feels able to try.
sharedPlan: Plot and record growth on the UK-WHO chart
Family meals; small portions of new foods beside accepted foods; repeated tries without pressure
No force, bribes or battles; short, calm meals
Set snack times; limit juice and large milk drinks between meals
Daily vitamin A, C and D drops for under-5s (Healthy Start if eligible)
safetyNet: Return if weight loss, falling centiles, a narrowing diet, choking or vomiting, or developmental concerns
Health visitor growth recheck in a few months

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost by over-investigating a well child, by skipping the growth chart, and by advice that increases pressure. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Reassuring without weighing, measuring and plotting.
items.why: Growth is the evidence of adequate intake; without it, reassurance is guesswork (NICE NG75).
items.fix: Plot weight and height on the UK-WHO chart and show the parent.

items.fail: Ordering blood tests or a multivitamin prescription for a thriving child.
items.why: Tests add distress and rarely help; standard vitamin drops are advice for all under-5s, not a treatment.
items.fix: Explain why tests aren’t needed; recommend the standard A, C and D drops.

items.why: Extreme restriction with distress, or social communication concerns, need assessment (NICE CG128).
items.fix: Ask how she reacts to new foods and about talking, play and nursery.

items.why: Grazing, juice and large milk drinks reduce appetite at meals.
items.fix: Take a full day’s food and drink history and set snack times.

items.fail: Advising the parent to insist the child finishes her plate.
items.why: Pressure and bribes worsen refusal and the battles.
items.fix: Recommend repeated, calm exposure and letting the child decide how much to eat.

items.why: Falling centiles or narrowing intake need review.
items.fix: Name specific triggers, involve the health visitor, and use teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Orders blood tests or prescribes a multivitamin without plotting growth; tells the parent to “make her eat it”; no red-flag screen or safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Plots growth, screens red flags, reassures that fussy eating is common, and gives practical no-pressure feeding advice.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: engages the child; distinguishes ordinary fussiness from ARFID and developmental concerns; addresses milk and juice grazing; gives correct UK vitamin advice; supports the parent’s confidence; involves the health visitor; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Let’s do some blood tests to check she isn’t deficient.”
avoid.instead: “Her growth tells us she’s getting enough; she doesn’t need blood tests.”
avoid.why: Tests in a thriving child add distress and rarely change management.

avoid.dont: “Just don’t let her leave the table until she eats it.”
avoid.instead: “Offer it, let her decide, and keep it calm.”
“All under-fives are advised to have daily vitamin A, C and D drops.”
avoid.why: UK advice recommends vitamin drops for children aged 6 months to 5 years.

Weighs, measures and plots on the UK-WHO chart; no blood tests when thriving.
Normal food neophobia versus faltering growth, ARFID, allergy, coeliac disease and developmental conditions.
Screens swallowing problems, GI symptoms, food reactions, development and extreme distress.
Common, normal fussy eating in a thriving child.
Practical low-pressure feeding advice agreed with the parent; standard daily vitamin drops for under-5s.
Addresses parental anxiety and family meals; health visitor support.

social.t: Daily mealtime battles strain the whole family. Reducing pressure helps the parent as much as the child.
Making separate meals and throwing food away costs money. Healthy Start can provide free vitamins and help buying food for eligible families.

legal.t: A parent with parental responsibility consents for a 3-year-old. Speak to Mabel directly on the call in a way she understands.

professional.t: Reassurance based on plotted growth is evidence, not dismissal. Record the measurements and centiles.
The health visiting team offers feeding support and growth checks, and should hear about any concern about growth or development.

community.t: Health visitors and children’s centres run feeding and parenting support. The NHS Start for Life website has advice on fussy eating.

redFlags: Faltering growth or weight loss (NICE NG75)
Choking, gagging, pain on swallowing, vomiting, diarrhoea
Reactions to foods (NICE CG116); coeliac symptoms (NICE NG20)
Extreme restriction with distress (possible ARFID); developmental or social communication concerns (NICE CG128)
ice: Idea: she is missing vitamins or something is wrong
Concern: she is not getting enough nutrition

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is normal fussy eating in a child who is growing well and developing normally.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Young children are programmed to be wary of new foods, a bit like a smoke alarm that goes off at anything unfamiliar. Each calm, no-pressure meeting with a food teaches the alarm it’s safe. Pushing sets the alarm off again.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried she isn’t getting enough and might need tests. Her growth chart shows she is getting what she needs, so she doesn’t need tests. What will help most is making mealtimes calmer.”
management.psychosocial: Relieve guilt, reduce the battles, and pick one or two changes the parent feels able to try.
sharedPlan: Plot and record growth on the UK-WHO chart
Family meals; small portions of new foods beside accepted foods; repeated tries without pressure
No force, bribes or battles; short, calm meals
Set snack times; limit juice and large milk drinks between meals
Daily vitamin A, C and D drops for under-5s (Healthy Start if eligible)
safetyNet: Return if weight loss, falling centiles, a narrowing diet, choking or vomiting, or developmental concerns
Health visitor growth recheck in a few months

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost by over-investigating a well child, by skipping the growth chart, and by advice that increases pressure. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Reassuring without weighing, measuring and plotting.
items.why: Growth is the evidence of adequate intake; without it, reassurance is guesswork (NICE NG75).
items.fix: Plot weight and height on the UK-WHO chart and show the parent.

items.fail: Ordering blood tests or a multivitamin prescription for a thriving child.
items.why: Tests add distress and rarely help; standard vitamin drops are advice for all under-5s, not a treatment.
items.fix: Explain why tests aren’t needed; recommend the standard A, C and D drops.

items.why: Extreme restriction with distress, or social communication concerns, need assessment (NICE CG128).
items.fix: Ask how she reacts to new foods and about talking, play and nursery.

items.why: Grazing, juice and large milk drinks reduce appetite at meals.
items.fix: Take a full day’s food and drink history and set snack times.

items.fail: Advising the parent to insist the child finishes her plate.
items.why: Pressure and bribes worsen refusal and the battles.
items.fix: Recommend repeated, calm exposure and letting the child decide how much to eat.

items.why: Falling centiles or narrowing intake need review.
items.fix: Name specific triggers, involve the health visitor, and use teach-back.
